diverge.why: CPython counts no allocations. Every primitive answers a level of live memory rather than a running total: tracemalloc.get_traced_memory gives current and peak bytes, sys.getallocatedblocks gives the blocks alive right now, and a tracemalloc snapshot counts the blocks that survived. A body allocating ten blocks and freeing them each iteration reads the same as one that allocates nothing.
diverge.remedy: A cumulative allocation counter in CPython, of the kind runtime.MemStats.Mallocs gives Go.

limits.what: Reads the current size of the memory that tracemalloc traces after gc.collect. It starts tracemalloc for the call when it is off, and reads the caller's trace when it is on. A thread that runs beside the call and keeps memory reachable adds that memory to each reading.
limits.why: tracemalloc traces the blocks of every thread of the interpreter and counts none per thread. Memory outside the allocators of Python, such as the buffers of a C library that uses malloc directly, is not traced.

limits.what: Checks the most bytes that are live at once during an iteration: the peak of the memory that tracemalloc traces, above the memory that was live when the iteration started, averaged over the iterations. A body that frees each block before it allocates the next counts one block, so the ceiling bounds the peak of an iteration and not the bytes that the iteration allocates in total.
limits.why: CPython keeps no running total of allocated bytes. tracemalloc.get_traced_memory returns the current and the peak traced memory, and sys.getallocatedblocks the blocks allocated now. Each of them is a level of live memory, and the peak is the one that a body's allocations raise and its frees do not lower.

limits.what: A zone resolves through zoneinfo, from the system's time-zone database or from the tzdata package, so a datetime in a zone can show another wall time than the definition's tzdata 2026e states. A zone that neither source has ends the read with a fault, and the text of the fault contains the name of the zone.
limits.why: CPython reads time zones from the platform, and Windows has no time-zone database without the tzdata package.

limits.what: A zone resolves through zoneinfo, as the prop.of entry states. An instant and a duration at nanoseconds decode to an int of nanoseconds. The decoder refuses a time-of-day, a local-date-time, a zoned-date-time and a wall-time at nanoseconds.
limits.why: datetime, time and timedelta have a resolution of one microsecond. Python states only an instant and a duration in nanoseconds, as the int that time.time_ns and time.monotonic_ns return.

A benchmark body here is inline, driven by a generator, so a setup closure would take the caller out of the loop they are already writing. It marks the setup in place with excluding instead.

The default build of CPython runs Python code on one thread at a time under the global interpreter lock, so a worker's latency includes its wait for that lock. tracemalloc reports one level of traced memory for the whole process, so no measurement attributes bytes to concurrent iterations.

records.artifact: The JUnit XML file that pytest --junitxml=PATH writes to PATH when the session ends.
records.location: One property element per record, in the order the records are made, under the properties element of the test's testcase element. Its name is the kind of the record followed by the record's number in its test, such as dokimi.assert.3 or dokimi.suite.1, and its value is the record's JSON. The testcase element names the test by its classname, the module's dotted path and the class, and its name, the function's name with its parameters.
records.status: The child of each testcase element: none for a pass, failure for a failed call, error for a failed setup or teardown, and skipped for a skip or an expected failure.
